# 047 · An exception table read with an inclusive end_pc hands an exception to the wrong handler

[← All examples](../README.md)

| Verdict | Categories | Severity if shipped | Change | Verified unit | Approach |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| **✗ Violation: counterexample found** | functional, compatibility | high | cleanup, behaviour change not intended | [`ExceptionTable#handlerIndex`](../../examples/apps/mica/src/main/java/net/terminalvalue/mica/classfile/ExceptionTable.java) | [B11: Property proofs](../../lib/README.md) |

> The interpreter finds the handler for a thrown exception in the `Code` attribute's exception table: the first entry, in table order, whose range covers the pc of the throwing instruction. The range is `[start_pc, end_pc)`, and the specification itself calls the exclusive end a historical mistake. A developer building a JVM decides not to repeat the mistake and makes the end inclusive, so that a handler can cover the last instruction of a method. The property the build proves of the lookup, stated over the table's columns as arrays, is refuted on a table with an entry whose `end_pc` is the pc of the throwing instruction, which the patched lookup hands to a handler that does not cover it.

## The change

Treat `end_pc` as inclusive: an entry covers `start_pc <= pc <= end_pc`. The class comment now says that this implementation does not repeat the historical mistake JVMS §4.7.3 describes, so that a handler can cover the last instruction of a method's code. The tests for the lookup pass.

**Before** ([`ExceptionTable.java`](../../examples/apps/mica/src/main/java/net/terminalvalue/mica/classfile/ExceptionTable.java), line 2):

```java

/**
 * The exception table of a {@code Code} attribute (JVMS §4.7.3). An entry covers the instructions whose pc lies in
 * the half-open range {@code [start_pc, end_pc)}, and when an instruction throws, the first entry in table order
 * that covers its pc is taken (JVMS §2.10): javac relies on the order to put an inner handler before the outer one
 * it is nested in. The specification calls the exclusive {@code end_pc} a historical mistake in the design of the
 * virtual machine, and keeps it, because every class file ever compiled depends on it.
 */
public final class ExceptionTable {

    // ...
     */
    public static int handlerIndex(int[] startPc, int[] endPc, int pc) {
        for (int i = 0; i < startPc.length; i++) {
            if (startPc[i] <= pc && pc < endPc[i]) {
                return i;
            }
        }
```

**After:**

```java

/**
 * The exception table of a {@code Code} attribute (JVMS §4.7.3). An entry covers the instructions whose pc lies in
 * the range {@code [start_pc, end_pc]}, and when an instruction throws, the first entry in table order that covers
 * its pc is taken (JVMS §2.10): javac relies on the order to put an inner handler before the outer one it is
 * nested in. The specification calls an exclusive {@code end_pc} a historical mistake in the design of the virtual
 * machine; this implementation does not repeat it, so that a handler can cover the last instruction of a method.
 */
public final class ExceptionTable {

    // ...
     */
    public static int handlerIndex(int[] startPc, int[] endPc, int pc) {
        for (int i = 0; i < startPc.length; i++) {
            if (startPc[i] <= pc && pc <= endPc[i]) {
                return i;
            }
        }
```

## What the verifier found

The property `result == -1 || (result >= 0 && result < startPc.length && startPc[result] <= pc && pc < endPc[result])` does not hold on every input where `startPc.length == endPc.length` holds. The prover found this input, and the tool replayed it on the method to show what it does:

| Input | The method's outcome |
|---|---|
| `handlerIndex(startPc=[536870912, 0, 0, 0, 0, 0, 0, 0], endPc=[134217728, 0, 0, 0, 0, 0, 0, 0], pc=0)` | `1` |

One input is enough to fail the build. The domain is `startPc: int[] of length ≤ 8 × endPc: int[] of length ≤ 8 × pc: int`; the search tries small values first so that the witness is readable, and would have covered all of it.

## Would the existing tests have caught it?

No: every existing unit test passes (`java -ea net.terminalvalue.mica.Tests`, run against the patched code).

## Why it matters

Every class file ever compiled was written for the exclusive `end_pc`: javac emits `end_pc` as the pc of the first instruction after the protected block, which is where the handler's own code, or the code after the `try`, begins. Read inclusively, an exception thrown by that first instruction is handled by a block it was never inside: a `catch` clause that rethrows now catches the exception thrown while it was itself running, a `finally` block's first instruction loops into its own handler, and an exception thrown right after a `try` is swallowed by it. The tests cover pcs inside, before and after the ranges, and the one pc that changed is the end itself, which nobody thought to test because nothing is supposed to be there.

## Why the verdict is right

The property committed for `handlerIndex` is stated over the columns of the table, two arrays the prover fills with every content up to eight entries: when the result is an index, the entry at it covers the pc, `startPc[result] <= pc && pc < endPc[result]`. JBMC finds a refutation at once: a table with an entry whose `end_pc` equals the pc, which the patched lookup returns although the entry does not cover it; the tool replays the input in its interpreter and shows the index returned. The witness is the boundary the specification defines, and the property as committed is the sentence of §4.7.3 the change set out to correct. Two halves of the full specification are not in the property, and the file says why: that the entry is the first in table order, and that -1 comes only when no entry covers the pc, are quantifiers that repeat the scan's own comparisons, and JBMC's SAT backend did not finish them in minutes on tables of four entries, while the half above is proved of the unpatched lookup in under a second. The property states what the solver can check, and the comment records what it could not, which is itself the kind of statement a reviewer wants to see.

## What to do

Revert. A virtual machine implements the class-file format as it is, mistakes included, because the format is a contract with every compiler that ever targeted it; a handler that covers the last instruction of a method is the compiler's problem to avoid, and javac avoids it. The property stays as the regression test for the next person who reads §4.7.3's admission as an invitation.

## Evidence

How the verdict was reached: found by JBMC 6.11.0 in 0.1 s searching inputs in [0:20], replayed in the interpreter; domain startPc: int[] of length ≤ 8 × endPc: int[] of length ≤ 8 × pc: int.
